newsitem.title: USA: U.S NAPM index drop signals economy growing slowly.
newsitem.headline: U.S NAPM index drop signals economy growing slowly.

text.p: A decline in an index gauging activity in the nation's manufacturing sector indicates that the U.S. economy is still growing, but more slowly than its brisk pace last spring, analysts said.
The National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index read 50.2 in October, down from 51.7 in September.
A reading above 50 points to an expanding economy.
The NAPM also said its new orders index fell to 51.6 from 56.3, its price index fell to 47.1 from 51.2 and its employment index edged down to 45.5 from 46.9.
"The numbers were more favorable than expected and the price component fell below 50," said Steve Ricchuito, chief financial economist at BZW Securities.

"I think it's just one more piece of information suggesting that the economy has moderated to a more sustainable pace and that strains on resources remain dormant right now," said Joshua Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust.

Despite what should have been a fairly friendly reading for the bond market, bond prices erased the gains made earlier on news that U.S. non-farm payrolls grew only moderately in October after shrinking in September.

Fifty minutes after the NAPM report was released, the 6-3/4 percent 30-year Treasury bond was down 10/32 to 101-1/32, yielding 6.67 percent. Before the NAPM release, the 30-year Treasury bond had been up 13/32.

"You might have expected the market to keep going up," said Ricchuito. "(The market's retreat) just shows that maybe more people got involved yesterday and that as we go into the election and the ($38.5 billion quarterly Treasury) refunding, people are a little more cautious at these levels."

"We have come a long way and the market has properly adjusted to a neutral Fed, a moderate rate of growth and dormant inflation pressures," said Feinman. "But where do we go to from here? For the market to go higher, it has to start pricing in an ease and that is way premature."
Feinman said another factor that might be putting a brake on the market is event risk.
"Next Tuesday is the (U.S. Presidential) election," said Feinman. "There is that gnawing concern that you could get one-party control of the government."
"If you got a Clinton victory, coupled with Republicans retaining at least one chamber of the Congress, the market would accept that as status quo," said Feinman.
"The refunding is out there (next week), too," he said.
But the crux of the market's inability to move higher is that it has priced in a neutral Federal Reserve policy and needs to contemplate an easing move to extend its advance.
At the moment, no evidence suggests that an easing move is more than a distant prospect, analysts said.
